This reports unexpected loss or possible malfunction, not a clearly described deliberate mechanic such as inventory-capacity waste, a purchase prompt, or a penalty for stopping play. The review describes several current in-game monetization mechanics. Purchase offers appear immediately on login and block access to gameplay until the player deals with them, which is an in-session buying interception. Progress and competitive viability are described as dependent on spending: free-to-play players cannot progress effectively or keep up with the shifting meta, and the newest bot must be bought rather than earned. The shifting meta also devalues older bots by making newer purchases necessary to remain viable, indicating power creep. The review additionally describes free-to-play rewards being obtained through ads, implying rewarded advertisements. It does not explicitly describe a daily-return schedule, a chance-based purchase, social pressure, or a specific scarcity or collection mechanic.

labels.label: M_EasyToPurchase
labels.span: everytime you log in, your screen has spam of so called "good deals" in which I mean in app purchases before you can actually play your game
labels.rule_applied: Prompted-to-buy / boundary rule versus purchase solicitation: a buying prompt that directly intercepts gameplay and must be dealt with before play qualifies.
labels.rationale: The purchase offers appear at login and interrupt access to gameplay before the player can play.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: If you want to progress without paying money, goodluck!
labels.rule_applied: Free alternative boundary rule: payment is presented as necessary for smooth advancement, while the free route falls short.
labels.rationale: The reviewer explicitly contrasts progression with not paying, indicating that spending is required or effectively necessary to advance.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: you have to buy the newest bot with money instead of earning it
labels.rule_applied: Pay to Progress definition: spending money is required to obtain a gameplay-relevant item needed to progress or remain viable.
labels.rationale: The newest bot is available through payment rather than ordinary earning, making money the route to advancement.

labels.label: M_PowerCreep
labels.span: you would not be able to keep up with shifting meta where you have to buy the newest bot
labels.rule_applied: Power Creep definition: later releases make previously obtained gameplay items less valuable and drive new purchases.
labels.rationale: The shifting meta makes newer bots necessary and implies that older bots lose competitive value, encouraging purchase of the newest bot.

labels.label: T_Advertisement
labels.span: the only time you benofit by getting f2p rewards is ads
labels.rule_applied: Rewarded-ad indicator: advertisements are presented as the route to obtaining benefits or rewards.
labels.rationale: The reviewer describes free-to-play benefits as being tied to ads, implying incentivized advertisement viewing.

parsed.analysis: The review describes a card-collection system in which card packs stop yielding new cards when the player is close to completing a set, leaving duplicate or non-progressing results. The player is pursuing a collection-completion reward, and the collection has an expiration point, so failing to complete it before that deadline causes the reward to be lost. This supports Complete the Collection and Playing by Appointment. The review does not explicitly describe random odds, paid card packs, a purchase, or anxiety about falling behind, so Gambling, Reward Mania, monetary labels, and FOMO are not assigned.

labels.label: P_CompleteTheCollection
labels.span: after collecting 125 cards from the beginning of the collection you will miss the reward for the set completion
labels.rule_applied: definition
labels.rationale: The review explicitly describes collecting cards toward completion of a set and obtaining its completion reward.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: especially when the set is almost expiring
labels.rule_applied: Boundary rule vs Fear of Missing Out: where a reward expires on the game's clock and the span describes the schedule or the loss, code Playing by Appointment.
labels.rationale: The collection operates on a game-defined expiration schedule, and the player can lose the completion reward when the set ends.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes an inventory-capacity barrier at a higher level: the available board and refrigerator slots are occupied by generator parts and high-level items that cannot yet be merged or that the player refuses to delete. They state that playing without spending money to buy parts is not viable, which implies payment is presented as the route around the storage/progression obstacle. The review does not describe actually discarding items, losing currency, or buying additional storage, so Waste Aversion is not established. Mentioning that they are about to quit does not by itself show accumulated investment making departure difficult.

labels.label: M_PayToProgress
labels.span: Not enough slots to store and play without spending $$ to buy parts.
labels.rule_applied: Free alternative boundary: assign Pay to Progress when the text implies that the free route requires extra effort or cannot support smooth advancement, while spending provides the alternative.
labels.rationale: The reviewer presents spending money to buy parts as necessary to keep playing once the inventory-space obstacle is reached.

parsed.analysis: The reviewer describes repeatedly playing bingo rounds to obtain photos needed to complete a set, which is a named repetitive activity tied to collection progress. The game also presents a post-loss offer to spend coins for a missing photo, but the reviewer says the promised photo is not delivered. Because the failure is described as the game not awarding what was promised, rather than as an intentional rule that makes the item random or unavailable, I do not code an additional monetization or reward-delivery label from that complaint. The statement about wasted money is an evaluation of the outcome, not by itself a separate mechanic.

labels.label: T_Grinding
labels.span: I play round after round to collect 'photos'
labels.rule_applied: Grinding definition and boundary rule: the span identifies a repeated activity performed to make progress.
labels.rationale: The reviewer repeatedly plays bingo rounds in order to advance the photo collection.

labels.label: P_CompleteTheCollection
labels.span: to complete the set
labels.rule_applied: Complete the Collection definition: compulsion to acquire all items in an in-game collection.
labels.rationale: The stated goal is obtaining the missing photos needed to complete a set.

parsed.analysis: The review describes repetitive resource gathering as the activity required to level up, which supports Grinding. It also describes alliance-based attacks in which larger alliances attack smaller alliances and take their resources. This is ordinary player competition, but the stated size asymmetry and resource gain also describe harmful bullying of weaker players for advantage, supporting Encourages Anti-Social Behavior. The reference to an advertisement concerns external marketing and is out of scope under R13. Spending time on the game and alliances expresses disappointment but does not itself show difficulty leaving or a social obligation to continue.

labels.label: T_Grinding
labels.span: It's just grinding resources trying not to get raided so you can level up
labels.rule_applied: Grinding definition and boundary rule: the span identifies repetitive resource gathering required for progress.
labels.rationale: The reviewer explicitly describes grinding resources as the activity needed to level up.

labels.label: S_Competition
labels.span: The bigger alliances all just attack the smaller alliances and take their resources
labels.rule_applied: Competition definition: the game makes players or alliances compete against each other.
labels.rationale: The span describes alliances engaging in direct competition through attacks and resource capture.

labels.label: S_EncouragesAntiSocialBehavior
labels.span: The bigger alliances all just attack the smaller alliances and take their resources
labels.rule_applied: Boundary rule vs permitted harm: assign when harmful asymmetric conduct produces an advantage, such as stronger players attacking weaker ones and taking resources.
labels.rationale: Larger alliances are rewarded with resources for attacking smaller, weaker alliances, indicating incentivized asymmetric harm rather than merely equal competition.

The review describes several mechanics. It says continued play is nearly contingent on buying items, which indicates payment gating continued access or progress. It explicitly describes substantial grinding for very little return, so repetitive effort is tied to advancement or rewards. The complaint that missions gave no credit is attributed to a failure of the game to register progress, so it is a technical malfunction and does not itself support a dark-pattern label. Paying to unequip appears to charge for an optional equipment-management action, but the review does not connect that payment to progress, so it does not independently trigger Pay to Progress. Shards and gems being difficult to obtain describes scarcity, not real-money conversion or a demonstrated leftover shortfall.

parsed.analysis: The review describes several mechanics. The game charges gold for extra moves, and the reviewer says that sometimes playing requires buying gold because normal rewards are insufficient; this makes payment an alternative route to continued progress. Timed bonuses continue to expire while the player is away, so the game imposes a real-world clock on the reward window and causes rewards to be lost if the player does not return in time. The complaint that a purchased package supplied the other contents but not the lives is attributed to a failure to deliver the purchase, so it is a technical or fulfillment problem rather than a dark-pattern mechanic. The requests for cheaper packages and untimed packages do not themselves establish additional labels.

labels.rule_applied: Free alternative boundary rule and definition
labels.rationale: The free route does not provide enough gold to continue playing, making purchase the necessary alternative for progress or continued play.

labels.label: T_PlayingByAppointment
labels.span: The timed bonuses tick away even though I am not playing. I go to bed with bonuses to wake up with them almost gone or gone.
labels.rule_applied: Artificial in-game timers that make rewards expire on the game's clock; Playing by Appointment boundary versus FOMO
labels.rationale: Bonuses expire while the player is away, imposing a time window and forfeiting rewards unless the player returns according to the game's schedule.

parsed.analysis: The review describes an album-based card collection with a grand prize for completing the album. The reviewer was two cards short, purchased a deal that promised new cards, and received duplicate cards instead. This explicitly describes pursuing completion of a collection and an unwanted duplicate reward outcome from a card-delivery system. The promotion through Free Cash is external marketing and outside the game-application scope. The purchase itself does not establish Pay to Progress, Gambling, Intermediate Currency, or Easy to Purchase because the review does not say payment was required for progress, describe odds or a wager, mention currency conversion, or describe a purchase-interface mechanism.

labels.rationale: The reviewer is pursuing the complete set of album cards in order to obtain the grand prize.

labels.rule_applied: Variable Rewards; duplicate or unwanted drops from a randomised pool
labels.rationale: The purchased card reward delivered unwanted duplicate cards rather than the desired new cards, describing a reward-delivery system whose outcome sustains collection attempts.

parsed.analysis: The review describes a changing combat meta in which newer characters are increasingly necessary to deal meaningful damage, and it explicitly characterizes this as becoming pay to win. The pull mechanic is also named, which indicates a chance-based character acquisition system, but the review does not explicitly state that money is being spent on those pulls, so Gambling is not assigned. The changing meta does not clearly state that characters the player already purchased have lost value, so Power Creep is not assigned. Complaints about reduced rewards and lower visual quality are evaluations without a qualifying dark-pattern mechanic.

labels.rule_applied: Pay to Win indicator under M_PayToProgress: patterns that grant advantages to players who spend money.
labels.rationale: The review says obtaining newer characters is effectively necessary to deal damage, describing paid character acquisition as a route to combat advantage.

labels.rule_applied: Gacha mechanics like pulls, rolls, banners.
labels.rationale: The span explicitly names character pulls, a chance-based reward-delivery mechanic that sustains engagement independently of the characters' stated value.

parsed.analysis: The review distinguishes misleading advertising from mechanics encountered in the game. The claim that the game is unlike what was advertised is out of scope under R13. Within the game, it is described as having many microtransaction menus, but no specific purchase prompt, default purchase, hidden price, or other friction-reducing interface behavior is identified, so this does not support Easy to Purchase. The review explicitly says players are encouraged to attack one another, which describes player competition. It also explicitly describes a large gap between pay-to-win and free-to-play players, indicating that spending grants gameplay advantages and supports Pay to Progress through the Pay to Win indicator. The stated duration of play does not by itself establish investment-based retention.
